events.excerpt: Hi all — EnsRationis from Robonomics. Sensors.social is an open environmental data network I designed, and it is now growing across the EU. Everything is open source: the Altruist sensors that feed it, the software that collects the readings, and the map. Web3 does one job here, the one it is good at: it settles the data as a common good anyone can check, not a vendor’s database. How it works on Robonomics Owners who choose to share their Altruist’s data join the network; each sensor has its own key and signs every measurement it sends. A connectivity node checks the signature and that the sensor has an active subscription on Robonomics, a parachain on Polkadot, then passes the reading to the live map. The node collects readings into batches, stores each batch on IPFS and writes its hash to Robonomics. Anyone can fetch a batch and check it against the chain. The network is federated: a city or a lab can run its own connectivity node, and its sensors still show up on the common map. Next, with Robonomics 5.0: the reading the sensor signed goes on chain itself, so there is no need to trust the node at all. Try the map: https://sensors.social Happy to hear from anyone who wants to run a sensor in their city or build on the data. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic
events.headline: Sensors.social: an open air-quality network on Polkadot is growing across the EU

events.excerpt: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks . When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal
events.headline: Git security vulnerabilities announced

events.excerpt: Long before smartphones became the pocket-sized computers we know today, the T-Mobile Sidekick was giving people a taste of the future. Released in 2002, it featured a full QWERTY keyboard, instant messaging, and push notifications at a time when most phones were still using multi-tap texting. But the Sidekick had one major weakness: it depended heavily on Danger's servers, which shut down in 2011, leaving the devices with much of their functionality permanently disabled. Or at least that's how things stood until Ashe decided to bring the Sidekick back to life . More than two decades after its debut, this hardware hacker has cracked its security system, built a browser-based simulator, and started recreating the long-defunct backend services. The first challenge was getting custom software running on a real Sidekick 3. DangerOS, the phone's Java-based operating system, only accepted applications signed by Danger or an authorized carrier. Developers could once obtain special keys to bypass this restriction, but that program disappeared along with the company. After tracking down an archived software development kit and factory firmware images, Ashe discovered that Danger's developer certificates relied on a 512-bit RSA key. That was a relatively modest security measure even in the

events.excerpt: The Nintendo Wii might be pushing 20 years old, but its classic motion-sensing remote still has plenty of life left in it. Sure, it may not be much use for playing the latest games, but that doesn't mean it has to spend the rest of its days collecting dust in a drawer. Electronics enthusiast GreatScott! decided to give one of these aging controllers a second chance by transforming it into an AI-powered universal remote that can control appliances around his house simply by pointing at them. Unlike standard universal remotes, which require users to memorize button combinations or scroll through menus, GreatScott!'s creation uses a camera and machine learning to figure out what it's pointing at. Aim it at a lamp, television, or roller shutter, press the Home button, and the remote identifies the target. A quick beep confirms recognition, and pressing the A button sends a command to toggle the appliance. This is made possible with the help of a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3 Sense development board, which includes a camera, Wi-Fi connectivity, and enough processing power to run a small neural network. GreatScott! paired it with a custom-trained image classification model that recognizes seven different scenes, including an unknown category for anything that doesn't match. To train the mo

events.excerpt: Ripple XRP fell to $1.05 on Tuesday within five minutes of the U.S. October consumer price index (CPI) report, which showed XRP USD price rising faster than economists expected. XRP crypto traded at $1.0797 when the report came out at 8:30 a.m. in New York, or 13:30 UTC. By 13:35 UTC it had touched $1.0500 on Binance, a 2.8% drop and its lowest price since August 19. It has since bounced to about $1.07. Bitcoin fell with it, dropping to $73,525 in the same five minutes. The drop puts XRP back on a level it has tested before. events.excerpt: Giving a robot an instruction is the easy part. Getting it to understand what you actually mean is a lot harder. Tell a household robot to bring you a cup of coffee, for example, and it might happily carry it right over your expensive laptop. You never told it not to, after all. Researchers have now developed a new system called FLEX that could make correcting these kinds of mistakes as simple as telling the robot what it did wrong. FLEX, or Flexible Feature Editing Pipeline, was developed by a group of researchers at MIT and NYU. Rather than using language only to tell a robot how to perform a task, the system uses natural language corrections to help it figure out which parts of the environment actually matter. That distinction is important because demonstrations can show a robot what behavior you prefer, but they don't necessarily explain why. If you demonstrate a path that keeps a cup of coffee away from a laptop, the robot might learn that the laptop should be avoided. What it may not understand is that you really want it to keep liquids away from electronics in general. FLEX tackles the problem with three operations: ADD, GENERALIZE, and MASK. ADD introduces a feature that the robot wasn't previously considering. GENERALIZE expands a specific feature into something broader,
events.headline: Teaching Robots What Really Matters

Sure, you can play classics like Donkey Kong and Street Fighter on just about anything these days, but there's something special about standing in front of an arcade cabinet with a joystick and a bunch of oversized buttons. Unfortunately, arcade machines are big, heavy, and not exactly something you can throw in the car for a weekend getaway. Maker Michael Alm came up with a clever solution to that problem by building a two-player arcade cabinet that folds up like a briefcase. Alm's portable arcade machine packs everything needed for some old-school gaming into a portable wooden enclosure. When opened, the upper half is equipped with a 15.6-inch LCD monitor, while the lower half houses two sets of arcade controls. Once it's time to pack up, the screen folds down over the controls, and a carrying handle makes the whole thing easy to transport. The system is powered by a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ running Batocera, a Linux-based operating system designed for retro gaming and emulation. It also needs to connect individual entries, current-period totals, and sealed periods when reconciling customer funds. An institution-level aggregate does not provide those per-account records. events.excerpt: From snapshots to streams A sensor-facing agent may need to respond not just to the latest reading, but to an event that began many windows earlier, a running count, or a rule that changed while data kept arriving. That is the problem behind TimeOmni-Live, a model evaluated using LiveTS-Suite, a benchmark for Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding. The full paper describes a shift from one-shot analysis of fixed inputs toward maintaining state over an open-ended stream. The associated arXiv record identifies the same version, dated Nov. 6, 2026. Unlike a fixed-window model that receives a bounded sequence and stops, a continuous system must decide whether to respond as chunks arrive, preserve useful history, and incorporate queries or revised instructions during the stream. The benchmark tests those demands through tasks built around continuing streams and evolving instructions. What the benchmark asks LiveTS-Suite contains 5,249 streams, 15,555 annotated response events and 2.2 billion timesteps, organized into 18 tasks across six capability groups. The sequence begins with instantaneous conditions, such as recognizing a threshold, and sequential conditions that require multiple observations. events.excerpt: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible. Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize. Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?
